summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the IAB. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1280 and RFC 2200.

eli5.summary: It is an old scoreboard of which Internet rules were official. Newer scoreboards replaced it.

subtitle: The authoritative guide to the standardization state and status of Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed a central authority to track which protocols are standardized, which are experimental, and which have become obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB publishes a quarterly list that categorizes all major Internet protocols by their development state (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, historic) and requirement level (required, recommended, elective, limited, not recommended).
tldr.outcome: RFC 1250 provided clarity on protocol maturity and interoperability requirements. RFC 1280 and RFC 2200 replaced it with updated listings as the protocol suite evolved.

facts.label: Implementation requirement
facts.value: 2+ independent implementations to advance to Draft

today: RFC 1250 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1280 and later by RFC 2200 as the standards process continued and new protocols were added or moved through the standardization track. These successor documents provide the current official standards listings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1250 is the IAB Official Protocol Standards document from August 1991, published by the Internet Activities Board (IAB) to record the standardization state of protocols used on the Internet. It describes the standards process itself, explains key terminology, and provides definitive lists of protocols in each category of development.

This was intended to be a living document, issued quarterly, so readers would always have the current view of which protocols were on track for standardization and which had been retired. The RFC itself notes that copies should be obtained from the Network Information Center or IANA to ensure they are current.
sections.eli5: This is an official scoreboard that says which network rules are official, which ones are still being tested, and which ones are too old. The IAB updates it four times a year so people know what is current.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
RFC 1250 details how protocols move through the Internet standards track. Most protocol development happens in the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) working groups. When a protocol is ready, it enters the standards track as a Proposed Standard. The IAB imposes minimum delays: at least 4 months before promotion to Draft Standard and 6 months before becoming a full Standard.

At each step, the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) must recommend advancement, and the IAB must ratify it. The RFC notes that advancement to draft standard generally requires at least two independent implementations, and advancement to standard requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability. Protocols may also be designated Experimental (for research work), Informational (specifications from other organizations), or Historic (superseded or no longer used).
sections.eli5: A new protocol starts as 'proposed,' then after testing becomes 'draft,' then finally 'standard.' Some protocols stay experimental, and old ones are marked 'historic' when they are replaced.

sections.title: Protocol States and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Every protocol in the RFC has two classifications. The first is its state: Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic. The second is its status or requirement level: Required (must implement), Recommended (strongly advised), Elective (optional), Limited Use (for specific cases), or Not Recommended (avoid).

The RFC explains that there is no single requirement level that applies to all systems, because systems vary widely—a requirement for a mail server may not apply to a terminal. Therefore, the RFC includes additional applicability statements and points to separate requirements documents (such as Gateway Requirements and Host Requirements) for detailed guidance.
sections.eli5: Each rule gets two grades: where it is in development (official or still experimental), and how important it is to implement (must have, should have, or optional).

sections.title: Reference Documents and Organization
sections.content:
RFC 1250 points to several companion documents maintained by IANA and the RFC Editor: the Assigned Numbers RFC (protocol codes and port assignments), the Annotated Internet Protocols RFC (known problems and experiments), Host Requirements (RFC 1122 and 1123), and Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009). The RFC also notes that DoD publishes MIL-STD specifications for IP, TCP, FTP, SMTP, and Telnet that are intended to describe the same protocols as the RFCs, and advises using both sets of documents together.

The bulk of RFC 1250 is organized by protocol category: Standard Protocols, Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols, Experimental Protocols, Informational Protocols, and Historic Protocols. Each section lists the relevant RFCs and indicates recent changes or new entries.
sections.eli5: The document points to other guides (like a book of assigned numbers and a requirements manual) and organizes protocols into groups based on whether they are standard, experimental, or old.

sections.title: Historical Significance and Successor Documents
sections.content:
RFC 1250 served as the authoritative reference for protocol standardization status in 1991. It lists contact information for the IAB, IETF, IRTF, IANA, the RFC Editor, and the Network Information Center, providing the governance structure for the Internet standards process at that time.

This RFC is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1280 (issued later in 1991 with more recent listings) and RFC 2200 (issued in 1997 with broader updates). Newer editions of the standards document have been issued regularly to keep pace with protocol evolution, but RFC 1250 remains a snapshot of the standardization landscape in August 1991.
sections.eli5: This was the official rule scoreboard in 1991. Later updates (RFCs 1280 and 2200) replaced it as new rules were added or old ones were replaced, but this document shows what was official back then.
